newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Group reshuffle gives CKI new identity.
newsitem.headline: Group reshuffle gives CKI new identity.

text.p: A reshuffle of Hong Kong tycoon Li Ka-shing's Cheung Kong group will give its infrastructure unit a diverse earnings base and the ability to become an independent power producer, analysts said on Wednesday.
Hutchison Whampoa Ltd, a 45.36 percent held associate of Cheung Kong, will inject its 35.01 percent stake in Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd into Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd (CKI).

CKI will pay for the stake by issuing 886.21 million new shares at HK$21.15 per share to Hutchison. Parent Cheung Kong will also inject its 70.66 percent holding in CKI into Hutchison, which will issue 349.50 million new shares at HK$58.50 to pay for the CKI holding.
As a result, Hutchison will hold 84.6 percent of CKI.
"It is now clear that he wants to make (CKI) into a regional IPP (independent power producer) in Asia," Tom Chesser, director of regional power research at BZW Securities Asia, said.
"This bodes well for the company, but it is an intensely competitive industry in Asia."

Li said the acquisition would allow CKI to participate in Hongkong Electric's future development "which may involve further overseas power business, particularly within the Asian region as well as internationally". CKI is chiefly involved in China toll bridge, toll road and power projects.

"It is obvious that by injecting Hongkong Electric into CKI in terms of management and resources, one has quite a different animal, a more competitive, more positive entity," said Andrew Taylor, analyst at Asia Equity.
The synergy between the two companies should allow CKI to take on significant new projects, particularly outside China.

The reorganisation was launched by Hutchison last Friday when it acquired 7.75 million shares of Hongkong Electric at HK$26.50, pushing its stake in the utility just above the 35.00 percent and triggering a general offer for Hongkong Electric.
CKI's Hongkong Electric stake will be capped at 50.01 percent, with any acceptances of Hutchison's offer in excess of 15 percent to be kept by Hutchison.
"After the injection of Hongkong Electric, CKI's balance sheet will be strengthened, its NAV (net asset value) will be boosted, said Manfred Ho, senior investment analyst at CEF GC Brokerage.
He said CKI's NAV per share would rise to HK$18.33 from HK$15.22 before the injection of Hongkong Electric. The issue of new shares would also boost its market capitalisation.
"CKI's P/E (price/earnings ratio) will also fall to 16.5 times 1997 earnings from 27 times," added Ho.
However, while applauding the group reorganisation, some analysts were sceptical of some aspects.
"Most of Cheung Kong Infrastructure's earnings were coming from Green Island Cement, now two-thirds will come from Hongkong Electric," said Archie Hart of BZW Securities Asia.
Analysts also pointed out that the current high share price already fully reflects the infrastructure play's earnings for the next five years or more.
"Where is the upside for the share price?," asks Steven Brown, group head of research at NAVA SC Securities.

Analysts had also expressed some concern that Hutchison would be forced to reduce its stake in CKI to 75 percent from 84.6 percent to comply with exchange listing rules that 25 percent of the issued capital of the company be in public hands. However, Hutchison is seeking a waiver from the exchange.
